A report evaluating youth employment in Africa has revealed that the average worker welfare score among the continent’s young workers stands at 41 per cent.
An economist, Habtamu Edjigu, disclosed this on Wednesday during a virtual media briefing on the findings of a report by the African Centre for Economic Transformation (ACET), titled “The Hidden Jobs Crisis: Why Low Unemployment Masks Africa’s Youth Challenge.”
Mr Edjigu said the sectors employing young people offer the poorest-quality jobs.
He noted that the findings highlight the urgent need for African countries to create better jobs that offer decent pay, job security and dignified working conditions.
ACET’s Regional Job Scan Study was conducted in partnership with the Mastercard Foundation.
The report draws on evidence from workers and 33,000 firms across 46 countries, looking beyond headline employment figures to examine where young people work and whether those sectors provide quality jobs at scale.
According to the report, the score of 41 out of 100 does not mean that young people’s jobs fall short in every aspect.

“For many, the basics are in place: most keep standard hours, and about six in 10 of those asked hold a permanent contract,” the report reads.
“The gap opens when something goes wrong. Fewer than one in five have health coverage or social security to fall back on, about one in four get paid leave, and fewer than one in five have a union to speak for them. For most young Africans, work is steady but unprotected, a reflection of how much of it remains informal.”
Mr Edjigu outlined four policy recommendations from the report to create more and better jobs for Africa’s young population.
He urged African leaders and policymakers to invest in sectors where jobs already exist by improving worker productivity and extending social protection, such as health coverage and social security, to young people employed in foundational sectors such as agriculture, trade and food processing.
The economist said creating an enabling environment for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) would accelerate job creation.
He also recommended expanding high-potential industries and aligning training systems with labour market demands.
Mr Edjigu explained that directing investments towards fast-growing, high-productivity sectors such as information and communication technology (ICT), pharmaceuticals and logistics would improve working conditions and expand employment opportunities.
ACET’s Chief Executive Officer, Mavis Owusu-Gyamfi, said benefits such as health coverage, social security and paid leave are often associated with formal employment, which most young Africans lack.
“Contrary to views in some corridors of power, Africa’s young people are not idle,” Ms Owusu-Gyamfi said.
“They are working hard in jobs that just don’t pay enough, don’t protect them, and don’t lead anywhere.
“And until we measure success by the quality of work, not just the number of jobs, that crisis will stay hidden.”
She described Africa’s employment situation as a “hidden crisis”, noting that the continent’s unemployment rate stands at about 8.9 per cent, particularly when compared with other regions.
She noted that, according to the report’s welfare index, three in four young African workers are in insecure and non-wage employment.
The report’s Worker Welfare Index combines 12 indicators across four dimensions: wage income, working time, benefits and employment security, and job satisfaction.
Ms Owusu-Gyamfi reiterated that young Africans are working, but their jobs are not improving their livelihoods.
Meanwhile, ACET’s Head of Youth Employment and Skills, Mona Iddrisu, urged the media to hold governments accountable for their promises and announcements on job creation.
Ms Iddrisu said journalists should assess the quality of jobs whenever government agencies announce employment opportunities.
She said journalists should ask questions about social security, working hours, decent wages and health benefits.
She also stressed the need for female employees to have access to maternity leave.
Young Africans work more than their peers on other continents, according to a study released in February.
The Mastercard Foundation study estimated that 304 million young Africans (57 per cent) were working as of 2025, compared with about 48 per cent of young people in the rest of the world.
“At the same time, young Africans enter the labour market while still of school age between 15 and 17 to take up predominantly low-paying, informal, agricultural work, often before completing their education,” the study said.
